name: npm_upgrade_planner_agent
description: An AI agent that plans upgrades for a project's npm dependencies. A DO_WHILE loop runs one action per iteration, picked by code: scan the next queued version with the POST_scan MCP tool (scan_npm_package, through the Orkes MCP Gateway), ask an LLM to propose versions, or stop. The workflow keeps the state and checks every choice against fixed rules; the LLM answers at most 3 times. The workflow then runs a full assess_npm_package review of each accepted version as a parallel sub-workflow, and writes the plan from those assessments. Before saving: save scan_npm_package and assess_npm_package, create the secret dependency_tools_key (the MCP Gateway API key), and, for the optional GitHub issue, set up the main workflow's GitHub secret and environment variables.

inputParameters.queryExpression:
# prepare_agent_context: checks that the gateway offers the scan tool, turns the dependencies into
# text for next_action, and sets agent_loop's iteration cap.
# POST_assess is left out on purpose: after the loop, the workflow assesses each accepted version
# itself, as an assess_npm_package sub-workflow, which has no gateway time limit.
# The cap is 4 iterations per dependency plus 4, the worst case: each of the 3 LLM answers brings a new
# version for every dependency (so 4 scans per dependency), plus the 3 LLM iterations and the last one,
# which stops. e.g. 20 for 4 dependencies. A normal run needs far fewer, so the cap only ends a run if
# something is broken.
.allowedToolNames as $allowed
| [ (.tools // [])[] | .name ] as $toolNames
| {
    dependenciesText: (.dependencies | tojson),
    maxIterations: (4 * ((.dependencies // {}) | length) + 4),
    # Tools the gateway didn't list, e.g. a renamed route. Every scan would then fail.
    missingTools: [ $allowed[] | . as $n | select(any($toolNames[]; . == $n) == false) ]
  }

tasks.name: agent_loop
tasks.description: One action per iteration, picked by next_action: scan the next queued version, ask the LLM to propose versions, or stop. The planner's state lives in the workflow variable stateText.

loopOver.name: next_action
loopOver.description: Picks this iteration's action. When nothing is queued, it first reviews every choice against fixed rules and writes the status lines the LLM reads.

scan.name: call_npm_tool
scan.description: Optional, so a failed scan is recorded in the ledger as an error and the agent moves on instead of failing. The inline taskDefinition gives it 2 retries, 5 seconds apart, because a system task without a task definition gets none.

messages.message:
You choose versions for the dependencies of an npm project. The workflow scans every version you choose and checks it against fixed rules; you only choose.

You get the goal, then one status line per current dependency: its status ("acceptable as is", "must change", "must be replaced" or "couldn't be checked") and what its scan found; your current choice and whether it was accepted, and why not; and candidate versions taken from the scans.

Rules:
- Give one choice for every current dependency, including those already accepted.
- A choice is accepted only if its scan has data, the version isn't deprecated, its package isn't deprecated as a whole, and it has no HIGH or CRITICAL advisory of its own. Advisories in its dependencies don't block it: the plan fixes them with npm overrides.
- Prefer the smallest change: keeping the current version, then an upgrade in the same major version, then a new major version, then a replacement package.
- Use an exact version such as 4.17.1, never a range or "latest". For the same package, take the version from its status line or its candidates; never guess.
- Never choose a version the status line says was rejected.
- Choose another package only for a dependency marked "must be replaced": a maintained package that does the same job, at the newest exact version you know exists. Say in the reason that it needs code changes. A replacement has no current version to stay close to, so once it's scanned, switch to its npm latest version (listed first in its candidates) unless that one was rejected.

Respond with JSON only, in exactly this shape:
{"choices": [{"dependency": "the current package name", "packageName": "the package to use", "packageVersion": "its exact version", "reason": "one short sentence"}]}

loopOver.name: record_result
loopOver.description: Adds the result of the action next_action picked to the state: a scan, or the LLM's answer, checked, with the versions it adds queued. It reads only that branch, because a reference to a task the SWITCH skipped can return its output from an earlier iteration.

loopOver.name: save_state
loopOver.description: Keeps the planner's state in the workflow variable stateText, which next_action reads in the next iteration and check_recommendations after the loop, instead of relying on references to tasks in earlier loop iterations.

tasks.name: assess_if_needed
tasks.description: A guard around the dynamic fork. In mode "assess" (check_recommendations verified at least one recommended version), it runs assess_recommended_versions and join_assessments. In mode "none" (the planner recommended nothing, or no recommended version had a clean scan), it skips them, so the run never starts a dynamic fork with an empty task list, which might fail the whole run. write_plan then marks each dependency "Not assessed", and the plan is still written.

assess.name: assess_recommended_versions
assess.description: Runs one assess_npm_package sub-workflow per verified version, in parallel, from the task list that check_recommendations builds. Sub-workflows, not the POST_assess MCP tool, because the MCP Gateway cuts calls off at about 60 seconds. Each one is optional, so a failed assessment doesn't stop the others.

inputParameters.queryExpression:
# summarize_assessments: pairs each recommendation with the result of its assessment: the verdict, the
# route and its reasons, what still needs fixing, and the full brief.
#
# Inputs:  .recommendations   from check_recommendations
#          .assessments       join_assessments' output: one entry per sub-workflow, keyed by its
#                             reference name (e.g. "assess_rec_1"). null when assess_if_needed
#                             skipped the fork because nothing passed the checks
# Output:  recommendations, each with an assessment (null if it wasn't assessed), and the same list
#          as JSON text for write_plan
(.assessments // {}) as $results
| [ (.recommendations // [])[]
    | . as $rec
    | (if $rec.assessmentRef == null then null else $results[$rec.assessmentRef] end) as $out
    | $rec + {
        assessment: (
          if $rec.assessmentRef == null then null
          # A sub-workflow that failed has no route. It's optional, so the others carry on.
          elif ($out.route // null) == null then
            {error: "the assessment failed or returned no route", workflowId: ($out.subWorkflowId // null)}
          else {
            verdict: $out.aiVerdict,
            route: $out.route,
            routeReasons: ($out.routeReasons // []),
            rejectReasons: ($out.rejectReasons // []),
            upgradeStatus: $out.upgradeStatus,
            recommendedVersion: $out.recommendedVersion,
            vulnerableDependencies: [ ($out.vulnerableDependencies // [])[] | {package, highOrCritical, fixedIn, fix} ],
            briefMarkdown: ($out.briefMarkdown // ""),
            workflowId: ($out.subWorkflowId // null)
          } end)
      } ]
| {recommendations: ., recommendationsText: tojson}

messages.message:
You write the summary at the top of an npm upgrade plan: one paragraph of at most 120 words, in plain sentences. The workflow shows the goal status just above your paragraph, and the overview table and every assessment's brief below it, so never repeat the goal status, and never include a table, a list, a heading or a section per package.

Use only the goal status, the overview and the scan problem you're given, and never contradict them. The workflow decides the goal status; never decide it yourself.
- If the scan problem isn't empty, start with it.
- Name the main actions, including overrides, and why a dependency is replaced. The overrides in a row fix those dependencies' HIGH or CRITICAL advisories, so never call them unresolved. For a row with no verified recommendation, say that it needs attention and why, and never suggest an action for it.
- For each version that needs a reviewer, say what the reviewer has to decide, from that row's reasons, such as whether its overrides are safe to apply. Only an override the row marks "(new major)" crosses a major version and may break the package that depends on it; never mention major versions otherwise.

Respond with JSON only, in exactly this shape:
{"summary": "the paragraph"}

body.title: npm upgrade plan (agent run ${workflow.workflowId})
